input: In this study, the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to formaldehyde is investigated, with a particular focus on the important question of catalyst form. Two different forms of the catalyst were compared, namely a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet, using one feed composition. The space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), was selected as the principal performance measure. The tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, with a hydrogen-to-carbon-dioxide feed ratio of 3. The results were striking. The monolith achieved a space-time yield of 0.64 kg L-1 h-1 together with a pressure drop of only 0.19 bar, and it lost 7% of its activity after 100 h on stream. The pellet, by contrast, achieved a space-time yield of 0.34 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.03 bar, and it lost 13% of its activity after 100 h. It is clear from these results that the monolith outperforms the pellet across the board, delivering a higher yield while at the same time imposing a lower pressure drop and retaining its activity more effectively. It should be noted, however, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and it is also worth bearing in mind that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the literature, which makes direct comparisons of this kind particularly valuable. Taken together, the findings provide a sound basis for preferring the monolith in this service, and they point the way towards further work in which the behaviour of both forms can be examined over considerably longer periods on stream.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen are converted over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to formaldehyde, and the catalyst form fixes both the yield of a reactor and the pressure drop it imposes. Two forms of the catalyst were compared on one feed composition: a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Tests ran at 280 °C and 40 bar with a hydrogen-to-carbon-dioxide feed ratio of 3. The monolith gave the higher space-time yield (0.64 kg L-1 h-1) at the lower pressure drop (0.19 bar), and lost 7% of its activity after 100 h. The pellet gave a space-time yield of 0.34 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.03 bar, and lost 13% of its activity after 100 h. The monolith leads on all three reported measures at the tested conditions, and the yield advantage does not have to be bought with pressure drop. The activity losses set the expected service behaviour: the monolith also loses activity more slowly, so its advantage at the start of a run is not one that the pellet recovers later in the run. For catalyst selection at these conditions, the structured form is the one the data support, since a higher space-time yield is a smaller catalyst volume for the same duty and a lower pressure drop is a lower compression duty on the feed. The comparison is bounded in two ways. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so tolerance to sulfur is unknown for both forms. And yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature, so the paired comparison made here, on one charge and one feed, is the basis for the preference.
